data.content_ref: inline:The target's pragmatic defense rests on a universal exclusivity claim that is empirically false. The mechanism asserts evolutionary theory-selection is 'the only strategy that doesn't lead to immediate extinction (error).' But 'only' is a strict universal: any alternative epistemic strategy that also avoids immediate extinction falsifies the claim. Dogmatic adherence to tradition, blind conservatism, random theory selection, or even non-selective pluralism all avoid 'immediate extinction' under the target's own loose criterion of not producing immediate error. Since survival-under-pressure is the sole justificatory standard the target invokes, and many heterogeneous strategies satisfy that standard, the evolutionary imperative cannot uniquely prefer Popperian severe-test selection over those alternatives. The pragmatic defense is therefore underdetermined by its own criterion: it establishes at most that SOME error-avoiding strategy is needed, not that THIS one is rationally privileged. Worse, the target's own countercondition concedes that 'adaptive fitness' may be 'indistinguishable from inductive success in practice,' yet the mechanism provides no operational criterion to separate them—so the 'not induction' claim is a bare relabeling rather than a substantive distinction. A defense that simultaneously (a) makes a false exclusivity claim and (b) fails to distinguish its proposed standard from the very inductive reasoning it rejects has no remaining justificatory force.
